extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and writers interested in history, literary criticism, and historical prose
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and implicit standards for producing and judging historical and literary prose: clarity, concision, handling of authorities, impartiality, diction, and rhetorical strategy. Drawn from a 19th-century literary review of a history book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good historian
rubrics_metrics.description: Great diligence in examining authorities, great judgment in weighing testimony, and great impartiality in estimating characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer praises Lord Mahon for these qualities and notes he 'does no more than justice to his ancestor Stanhope; he does full justice to Stanhope’s enemies and rivals.' These are presented as essential historian virtues: thorough source work, careful evaluation of evidence, and fairness even toward personal connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity and concision of narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: His narrative is very perspicuous, and is also entitled to the praise ... of being very concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity (perspicuity) and brevity (conciseness) are endorsed as important merits in historical writing; the reviewer treats concision as a rare and valuable quality in modern writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of words and idiomatic style
rubrics_metrics.description: He has not yet acquired a great command of words. His style is seldom easy, and is now and then unpleasantly stiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should cultivate a wide and flexible vocabulary and an easy, natural style; stiffness and limited command of words are faults that detract from otherwise good work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accurate terminology; prefer clarity over dogmatic purism
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not like to see French words introduced into English composition; but, after all, the first law of writing ... is that the words employed shall be such as convey to the reader the meaning of the writer. Now an Abbot is the head of a religious house; an Abbe is quite a different sort of person. It is better undoubtedly to use an English word than a French word; but it is better to use a French word than to misuse an English word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction should prioritize accurate meaning: do not substitute or anglicize words incorrectly for the sake of purism. If a foreign word is the correct term, it is preferable to an incorrect native substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sententious, oracular moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Too fond of uttering moral reflections in a style too sententious and oracular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral reflections should not be delivered as trite, overbearing pronouncements. The reviewer criticizes grandiose, 'oracular' maxims that have become banal, recommending restraint and freshness in moral commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental rule of writing: convey meaning to the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: The first law of writing ... is that the words employed shall be such as convey to the reader the meaning of the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is advanced as the overriding principle governing diction and style: clarity of communication trumps linguistic pedantry or adherence to fashionable usages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality even toward kin and personal connections
rubrics_metrics.description: He does no more than justice to his ancestor Stanhope; he does full justice to Stanhope’s enemies and rivals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A historian should avoid nepotism or biased praise/condemnation; fair treatment of friends, relatives, and rivals is evidence of sound critical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective argumentative strategy: use opponent's values
rubrics_metrics.description: The really efficient weapons with which the philosophers assailed the evangelical faith were borrowed from the evangelical morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing an opposing system, using its own moral premises and language can be an especially potent rhetorical strategy; this observation serves as guidance for persuasive critique and polemic.
